title: Aliens
creator: James Cameron
review: The perfect sequel, almost better than Ridley Scott’s masterpiece, only hindered by the heavy-handed sentimentality that signals the motherhood theme too overtly at the end. Most sequel films suck because they try to recapture what made the original great, which in film cannot be done since mimicry is the enemy of innovation. Aliens does not simply rehash Alien, and manages as a stand-alone film rather than just an installation in a franchise by progressing from the stalking tension of the first film to action-packed horror. But while Aliens makes enough thematic and atmospheric changes to distinguish itself, it is also brilliant in its retention and development of the ideas Alien first generated. The motherhood and sexual dynamics are turned up another notch as Ripley makes her symbolic adoption and confronts LV-426’s “queen” and as traditional masculine/feminine roles are subverted through the tough female characters and method of alien reproduction. This is an excellent film that is paced perfectly and brings many more new ideas than the simple addition of the ‘s’ to the title would indicate.

title: ドライブ・マイ・カー [Drive My Car]
creator: 濱口竜介 [Ryusuke Hamaguchi]
review: This film taught me that one important value of slow films is that the long silences and gradually advancing plot give space for feelings to really develop. Inconsequential scenes give time for contemplation of the plot-relevant scenes that precede them. This film is not the best example of this, it’s just the first where I found myself consciously noticing the effect. This film is really pointlessly slow, there are many empty scenes of ugly highway landscapes with banal music overlaid. I am fine with films being slow, but I do not appreciate filler content that does not even seriously contribute to atmosphere. This movie is quite ugly. Most contemporary films are tragically shot on digital, which makes them all look like the same porous hyperreality that could spring CGI on you at any moment. It is very apparent in this film, the long shots of which invite you to stare at actors’ faces in ugly styleless clarity. Love the dream shared between Kafuku, Oto, and Takatsuki. Invites much interpretation. The sole retribution Kafuku attempts on his wife for her infidelity is in refusing to give her the end of her dream-story. Takatsuki reveals that not only did Kafuku’s attempted payback fail, as Oto shared the same story with Takatsuki and therefore learned its plot, but that Oto did not share the ending with Kafuku at all, instead with Takatsuki in one of their trysts. The dream itself is a neat puzzle. The burglar is clearly Kafuku (damage to the left eye), but who are the girl and her prospective beau? I think the uncharacterised boy is also Kafuku, having seen the results of the iniquity performed in his own bed, but pretending that it never happened. If the girl is Oto herself, does she know that Kafuku has seen this infidelity? The girl confesses to the camera, and it is implied that Oto intended to do the same to Kafuku the night she died. Takatsuki is notably absent from this dream that she shares with him, pointing to his actual insignificance in her life; he is only one of many sex objects she uses for creativity’s sake. The girl masturbates in the boy’s bed, further removing Takatsuki from his role of sexual partner. Takatsuki has reason to envy Kafuku; Oto never had any love for him.

The only difference is that the protagonists lack pretense and actually seem to be having fun. The abuse of the American flag in the film (mostly as a handkerchief) is a microcosm of the film’s entire disregard for American icons, in the traditional sense of the word. The worst parts are the senseless violence and hallucinogenic special effects. Beautiful film by any metric, and an excellent performance by Depp. Final soliloquy and billboard are utterly insipid.

title: Festen [The Celebration]
creator: Thomas Vinterberg
review:
The relationship to one’s parents is one of endless submission. I write this in the months following the regular deaths of both grandfathers, over whom neither of my parents ever held the upper hand. Even now my father, despite perpetual disaffection, contends with feelings he could only ever put on hold. I am sure to do the same. Festen platforms the attempts of four children to revenge themselves upon their parents, a universal desire. They get closer than most: embarrassing, beating, and ultimately denying him their presence. But even for protagonist Christian, who succeeds in humiliating his father and uniting his family against him, there is nothing he can do to reverse his abuse. What does Christian gain from the night of revenge? Momentary satisfaction. What does Christian suffer? He suffers betrayal from his brother and mother, abandonment by his living sister, humiliations of his own. In the morning, spirits cooled, Helge gives a genuinely apologetic speech that none of his

children interrupt. Though he is ushered upstairs, he retains the last word, the right to solicit forgiveness. After all is said, they are still his children, they still bear the weight of family history and heredity.

title: Le deuxième sexe [The Second Sex]
creator: Simone de Beauvoir
review: Despite containing many inaccuracies, The Second Sex is widely regarded as the most seminal work in feminist literature. Its size and breadth of subject matter lend credence to this title, but its faults should not be ignored. De Beauvoir is not a biologist, but she makes a number of biological claims that are often speculative (such as her continued reference to hermaphrodites despite their near-nonexistence) or plainly wrong (for instance, her statement that more women than men die between the ages of fourteen and twenty-two, which is a statistical falsehood that has never been true of the general population. These inaccuracies detract from her credibility in every topic but philosophy, which requires no concrete evidence or facts, things de Beauvoir obviously struggles with. Furthermore, it seems at times that de Beauvoir uses meaningless statements to pad her book, such as “The tremendous advance accomplished by psychoanalysis over psychophysiology…” These koans bring confusion and distract from her main points. Her entire chapter of psychoanalysis is based on Freud, who is not nearly as respected now as he was then. The chapters on history are especially troublesome. With no footnotes to speak of, it no longer becomes a matter of refutation to disagree with de Beauvoir, but rather simple dismission, as the burden is on de Beauvoir to prove her claims, not the reader to believe her. Considering the size of her assertions, most of her book must be considered bunk for any purpose besides stimulating the imagination. De Beauvoir makes some valid and interesting claims, such as the idea that men are instilled with an autonomy early on that women are not by way of their urinary function, in that men can manipulate their penis and therefore master their urination, whereas women are more inclined to feel submissive to their bodily function. These insightful ideas are however overshadowed by a lack of evidence and the breadth of incorrect information present in the book.

title: Manhattan

review:
I think this film is clearly sequential to Annie Hall, but wanders a bit too much to be on the same level. Even more than in Hall, Manhattan is a brilliant marriage of confession and fantasy, where Allen can narcissistically expose his worst traits while cavorting with attractive women and

exercising his wit. This film plays Allen’s negativity stronger, distancing us from his character and ending on a sad note. It’s no coincidence that the book written about his character is a more accurate portrayal of him than the pretentious writing attempt the film opens with.

review: An appreciatively broad history that is too liberal in outlook to give “socialism with Chinese characteristics” (or the post-colonial African variant) its fair shake, though its scepticism is warranted for the various other perversions of Mao’s project. This book could have focused more on the Chinese context and the specifics of Tse-tung’s policies, given that these provide the entire impetus for Maoism’s global reach.

review: Goes just short of acknowledging the superiority of African socialism, acknowledging that Washington Consensus “efficiency” is not necessarily the best metric by which developing nations should be judged. Pretty even-handed, considering that it's a favourable appraisal of a successful socialist state under an admitted Liberal framework.

title: Megamind
creator: Tom McGrath
review: Much like its spiritual predecessor Incredibles, Megamind introduces the concept of trope deconstruction to children in a well-conceived and understandable manner, preserving a compelling plot along with its demonstrated themes and humour. Unfortunately, Megamind does not commit fully to the deconstruction; a mistake most obvious in Tina Fey’s character of Roxanne Ritchie who is a complete helpless damsel in distress. The ending also disappoints, with a musical number that accompanies a montage of all loose ends being cleaned up, which commits the cardinal sin of being a tired trope and kitschy. There are a collection of other tropes this film falls victim to, such as the in media res flash forward opening that the film returns to at the end or The greatest plot issue in this film is due in that much of the character development (most notably Ritchie’s swift development from hating to appreciating Megamind) feels rushed. This is in large part due to the ambition of the film seeking large, believable twists, subversions, and moral messages. If given more time and care, these character developments could become more believable. This would, of course, require a longer film, ultimately alienating it from its intended audience.

review: Confusing, clearly some sort of koan. Hard to keep track of the names, but that's Russian for ya. Always feels like you're on the verge of getting a clue, but it never arrives. Don’t confuse it for a surrealist piece á la Altman or Lynch; I don’t believe the essence of this film is transmitted through an emotional undercurrent caused by dreamlike passages. I think there is a conscious logic, or illogic, to the film, with wildly different scenes following each other to create distinct meaning. I don’t think this meaning is objective, the film is clearly open to many different interpretations, but I do think the film aims to create a puzzling narrative that can be consciously understood. It is not merely a set of scenes that must be understood unconsciously, as with a surrealism.

review: As with much of Monty Python and similarly Wildean or epigrammatic film, the jokes are funnier in theory than in practice. I suspect that the script is funnier than the film, simply because many of the jokes or gags are ill-delivered. Some of the jokes go too long or simply weren't funny to begin with. The density of jokes that Monty Python is known for is not present in this film, which is a major fault as a high quantity of jokes serves as quality assurance: failed jokes are forgotten as new jokes are presented. The story itself isn't very strong either. The irreverence of the film's nature doesn't excite as much as it prevents sticking to a strong plot line.

review: What a letdown following Manufacturing Consent. This book is no more than a weak addendum to that masterpiece. Where the Herman-Chomsky opus has concise examples, clear argument, and engaging structure, Necessary Illusions has examples that go on too long without reaching a defined point, a stagnant and vague thesis of “media serves power”, and is mystifyingly structured into a short text followed by a series of plotless appendices. This book could be simply formulated as a comparison of the case studies of US media treatment of Nicaragua and Israel. That’s all this book is. Instead, Chomsky flits between the two studies without rhyme or reason, alternating information about the case studies in nonsensical sequence.

title: Nightcrawler

review: A solid film idea with mediocre execution that could have benefited from an extra hour of characterisation and slower escalation to a more meaningful climax rather than the one-dimensional characters and rushed ending offered. The film's best qualities are Gyllenhaal’s acting and the satire of neoliberalism, with most of his lines being truisms such as “If you want to win the lottery, you have to work to make the money to buy a ticket” and “Do you know what fear stands for? False Evidence Appearing Real”, and rehearsed, work-fetishising lines such as “I know that today’s work culture no longer caters to the job loyalty that could be promised to earlier generations”, etc., but played to the extreme in an antisocial character. This is the best part of the film and should have been its focus. Nightcrawler mirrors a similar black comedy, American Psycho, in both its critique of high-level capitalism and failure to commit to its own excellent concept. Also clear is its directorial debt to Martin Scorsese films, especially Taxi Driver, with dragging shots of Gyllenhaal’s blank face in the car and the overwrought mirror scene.

Luckily the film has a steady upward trajectory following this point. Lowlights are Rocky and Adrian’s one-dimensional characters, the predictable plot, and lack of interesting shots. Highlights are the characters of Apollo Creed and Mickey Goldmill, legendary training montage, and final scene that makes it all worthwhile.

title: Rushmore
creator: Wes Anderson
review:
Never before have I been so conflicted about a film. On the one hand, I have a longstanding aesthetic predilection for homosociality, which this film explores with beautiful style and a veneer of innocence, such that the audience may discover friendship all over again. Furthermore, while I do not have so strong a fascination with boarding schools, I do have deep personal experience with them and this element of the film pulls at my heartstrings in a more personal way. So from a critical distance I can enjoy the core relationship of the film and appreciate the auteur cinematography, while I have a personal relationship with the setting. For all the faults that I will soon get to, the style is really a high point, as it is in all of Anderson’s films. Each room is like a model house with its nonverbal exploration of its denizen’s character. The setting speaks more than the characters do! But there is much that disappoints. For one, every single needle-drop is jarring and inappropriate. I have an appreciation for the tenets of the Dogme 95, but I am not an ideologue who opposes all

non-diegetic sound. The use of music in this film is simply amateurish: there are far too many songs, they overlay montages that deserve to actually be explored, the songs do not fit their scenes, and the songs themselves are generally poor. Additionally, we have a terrible mix of flat characters acting out a meandering plot. Ms. Cross is merely a means to an end: a loosely attractive young woman over whom our two protagonists may pine. Herman Blume wanders directionless through this movie, lost whenever he is unattached to Max, who himself is driven, but an empty vessel. We get glimpses of pathos: Max obscures his father’s profession out of shame, Blume betrays his friend for the woman. Just as often, however, we have unbelievable character beats like Blume’s abuse at the hands of his sons and Max’s easily resolved spats. Not much happens in this film that advances the characters’ goals or plot, but there are plenty of films where nothing important happens and there are no rules about what a plot should be. It is disappointing, however, when one is sitting and watching a story that continually proves there is no reason to believe an arc will resolve, one may be frustrated that the characters acting out this story are equally unattached to its outcome, merely wooden automatons that act it out. It would be Beckettian if it wasn’t so damn twee.

title: Sexual Personae: Art and Decadence from Nefertiti to Emily Dickinson
creator: Camille Paglia
review: While the giants on whose shoulders Paglia stands are extenuated by their positions at the beginnings of psychology, anthropology, and other social sciences, this author has no excuse citing works like The Golden Bough in 1990, long after their academic disaccredation. With propositions as droll as “cats are female animals” and “fascism is homoerotic”, Paglia is intentionally contrary to the point of senselessness. Sexual Personae’s strength is in psychoanalysis, though psychoanalysis reveals as much of the analyst as it does in the patient, as the analyst is the prism through which the neurosis is divined. A psychoanalysis applied to all humanity, this work reveals little about its subject due to reliance on bunk science, but a humanity’s worth about Paglia herself.

The worst parts are everything else.

The chapters jump between periods and narratives so frequently that I found no use in attempting to form a conceptual sequence of events. A “history of Rome” is simply too great a task for any single publication to accomplish, and this book ends up disjointed and spread thin over many concepts.

A few great shots that demonstrate that Wilder was doing more than just tell a story, especially that image of Norma staring down at Gillis through the cage he is about to willingly reenter, deceiving us into thinking he has truly come to accept his fate in the decaying mansion. The melodrama gets to be too much for me at the end, though.

title: The Age of Empire, 1875-1914
creator: Eric Hobsbawm
review: Though the end to Hobsbawm’s trilogy is not as strong as the previous two volumes, The Age of Empire cements his 19th-century history as the soberest I have read, encouraging a non-Marxist, non-Liberal materialist reading of Europe’s glorious century. The author’s weakly pessimistic view is justified by the eclipsing of technological and medical achievements by imperialism’s long shadow. The highlight of this book is Hobsbawm’s analysis of the causes of the great war, which distances itself from obfuscatory concerns regarding guilt, national ideology, or aesthetics.

title: The Age of Extremes, 1914-1991
creator: Eric Hobsbawm
review: Not without its blindspots and bias toward socialism, but a deeply thought-provoking book. Likely the weakest of Hobsbawm’s “Age of” books, but still one of the best attempts at global history that I have ever read.

title: The Age of Revolution, 1789–1848
creator: Eric Hobsbawm
review:
One of the most informative, best-written histories I have ever read. Hobsbawm takes on the Herculean task of summarising over half a century of general European history and pulls it off. His socialist perspective on history is invaluable, as he transforms historical materialism from

theory to actual analysis. This book is dry and dense, yet engaging it in its interface of the impact of Hobsbawm’s “dual revolution” to class development.

title: The Art of Self-Defense

review: Thematically strong but poorly executed, this film excels in gags that are far more disturbing than funny and flounders in soapbox morals so platitudinal as to detract from whatever restraint the film briefly exercises.

title: The Capital Order: How Economists Invented Austerity and Paved the Way to Fascism
creator: Clara E. Mattei
review: An interesting comparative political economy of English and Italian varieties of policy responses to the economic consequences of the first world war. I disagree with its expansive definition of austerity, which includes industrial policy and labour repression, and I find it lacks a “smoking gun” on the intention of economists to immiserate labour. Though I disagree with much of its analytical content, I find this book very thought provoking, it leads my mind to important questions like: if inequality is a necessary byproduct of the conditions necessary for economic growth, what tradeoff between public welfare and growth is optimal? Does fascism have an economic character or does it merely adopt and adapt to existing economic theories? Does democracy hamper or facilitate optimal economic policy?

review: Yet another poor holiday film. Not even Kurt Russell can save this film, as he earnestly performs a role as a band might play music on a sinking ship.

title: The Colour Out of Space

review: There are really only two interesting facets to this story. The first is the “blasted heath”, which is undoubtedly one of Lovecraft's best settings, and its description in the first few pages lays out a strong sense of foreboding. The second is the analogy to Sodom and Gomorrah: a location destroyed by a higher power for no discernable reason is contrasted to the biblical justice in the allegory, and the individual who dares look back on the destruction is punished, killed in the bible per the Old Testament’s theme of punitiveness, deranged in The Colour per Lovecraft’s narrative stock device.

title: The Fly
creator: David Cronenberg
review: Cronenberg’s body horror is not first-rate merely because of his dedication to imaginative practical effects; he uses it as an instrument to investigate existential notions of identity and desire. Here he takes a man on the path to inhumanity and asks: “When is a man no longer himself? When he behaves irregularly? When he ceases to resemble himself? When he believes himself something else?” At film's end, Goldblum’s character declares himself a Zhuangzi butterfly but elides the uncertainty central to the Daoist parable. While the viewer holds an ambivalent position toward his humanity throughout the film, as even at the end, the monster moves and emotes anthropomorphically, the character insists he is no longer human. Is this up to him to decide?

title: The Logic of Capital: An Introduction to Marxist Economic Theory
creator: Deepankar Basu
review: The economic thought of Karl Marx deserves to be taken seriously. Indeed, he may be one of history’s greatest thinkers on economics, even if most of his ideas, like the labour theory of value, have not stood the test of time. Deepankar Basu, a heterodox economist at the heterodox UMass Amherst Department of Economics, does an excellent job of extending Marx’s thought to modern methods with a minimum of deviation. This is an impressive feat because Marx wrote prior to essential conceptual/mathematical developments in economics such as the marginal revolution and development of econometric methods. Most who try to extend Marx to modern methods must make extreme alterations to Marx’s thought in order to maintain logical consistency, such as the analytical Marxists who dispensed with key features like dialectics and the aforementioned labour theory of value. This work remains as close to Marx’s thought as possible while adapting to advanced methods and developments, which is both its strength and its weakness. It is the best defense of Marxian economics that I have read, but its failure to convince me has led me to move on from orthodox Marxism as a workable framework.
